This paper proposes Spectral Contrastive Regression to improve both in-distribution and out-of-distribution regression. It introduces two novel losses: one minimizing the standard deviation of the feature-to-label distance ratio, and another aligning spectral norms between real and synthetically augmented distributions.  
The empirical evaluation is impressively thorough, showing state-of-the-art or near-state-of-the-art results across eight very diverse datasets spanning tabular, image, and time-series data. The design of the two loss components is practically motivated and computationally lightweight. Strongest evidence comes from the MPI3D analysis contrasting different norm choices, clearly supporting the spectral norm alignment choice.

However, there is a real and substantial weakness: the theoretical framing for the first loss (L_std) is overclaimed and technically unsupported. The paper asserts homeomorphism-based justifications and Lipschitz continuity that simply do not follow from minimizing the standard deviation of distance ratios. This gap undermines the core conceptual narrative of the paper. Additionally, while the fine-tuning strategy is borrowed faithfully from prior work for fair comparison, the absence of any ablation removing FT across the main benchmarks (where improvement is largest) prevents clean isolation of the novel losses' contribution. The minor issue of missing confidence intervals also weakens certainty, especially for modest reported improvements.

Overall, this paper reports a well-executed, empirically strong contribution with a clear and soundly-tested central algorithmic idea (especially L_svd). The primary weakness — overclaimed theoretical guarantees for L_std — can be fixed through reframing, but as presented, it is a notable lack of rigor. Given the consistent strong empirical showing combined with this theoretical overreach, the paper sits in the range of a weak accept: serious merit and useful results weighed against imperfect framing.
